title: Difficulty-Calibrated Interpolation Paths for Conditional Flow Matching

paper.title: Difficulty-Calibrated Interpolation Paths for Conditional Flow Matching
paper.abstract:
Abstract Conditional Flow Matching trains generative models by regressing a
network onto the velocity of a prescribed noise-to-data interpolation
path. The interpolation schedule that shapes this path is known to
affect convergence and sample quality, yet it is invariably fixed in
advance, independent of both the data and the model. We show that the
regression difficulty of Conditional Flow Matching varies
systematically along the path, and we propose Difficulty-Calibrated
Flow Matching, which derives the schedule from the model itself: a
short pilot run with the linear path records the per-time loss, and
the schedule is set to the quantile function of this difficulty
profile, so the trajectory lingers where the velocity is hardest to
learn. The method has a single hyperparameter, leaves the training
objective and its gradient equivalence intact, composes with
classifier-free guidance, and adds about two percent training
overhead. In controlled experiments on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and
Fashion-MNIST with an identical compact U-Net, the calibrated path
attains the best FID on CIFAR-10 at full sampling budget and clearly
outperforms all fixed schedules in the large-batch, few-update regime,
precisely the setting where compute is scarcest.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Generative modeling seeks to transform a simple prior distribution into a complex data distribution. Diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] and Flow Matching (FM) [ 4 ] have emerged as the dominant frameworks for this task, produced samples by integrating a learned time dependent velocity field, along an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] makes training docile and simulation-free, rather than regressing onto an stubborn field. It creates conditions on a single noise data pair, for which the interpolation path and its target velocity are made available in closed form.Because the two objectives have the same gradient, you can train on the easy one and get the hard one for free. That is the whole trick behind CFM. Interpolation schedule α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) determines the noise to sample moving path. This is the core of CFM. This α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) actively controls the training path convergence and sample quality [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Nevertheless,in every case the schedule is fixed a priori . This schedule is independent of the data and the model being trained of. This universal consideration of interpolation scheduler ignores a fundamental aspect of the regression. That is, it is not equally hard at every point along the path. Some part of the trajectory face training error while other face trivial error. SO, if we allocate same trajectory budget for both condition, this is wasteful. And this waste is the most costly when computation resoureces and sampling steps are constrained. We propose Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching (DC-FM), which derives the interpolation schedule from the model’s own measured difficulty instead of predetermined data independent priori (Fig. 1 ). We run a short pilot with the linear path and record the per-time pilot difficulty; because the linear target norm is constant in t t , this profile reflects genuine learning difficulty rather than a time-varying target scale. Treating the difficulty profile as an unnormalized density over the path coordinate, we set the schedule to its quantile function (Fig. 2 ). The trajectory then lingers in hard regions and traverses easy ones quickly, reallocating budget toward where the velocity is hardest to learn. A single emphasis exponent γ \gamma controls the strength of this calibration, with γ = 0 \gamma=0 recovering the linear path exactly. DC-FM requires no change to the CFM objective. The schedule is frozen before the main training run, so the gradient equivalence that underpins CFM continues to hold, and the method composes with classifier-free guidance [ 10 ] without modification. It is also distinct from non-uniform timestep sampling [ 8 , 3 ] , which alters which t t are trained on but leaves the inference trajectory unchanged; by reshape α \alpha , DC-FM instead rescales the target velocity and thereby the sampling dynamics themselves. Our contributions are as follows: • We show that the CFM regression difficulty varies systematically along the interpolation path, and that fixed a priori schedules spend trajectory budget uniformly regardless of this structure. • We propose DC-FM, a two-stage method that measures per-time difficulty in a pilot run and sets the interpolation schedule to the quantile function, that difficulty, governed by a single hyperparameter γ \gamma . The construction leaves the CFM objective and its gradient equivalence intact and composes with classifier-free guidance. • We evaluate DC-FM against linear (rectified-flow), cosine (GVP) and sigmoid schedules on CIFAR-10, MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under a strictly controlled budget, attaining the best FID@100 on CIFAR-10 (5.44 vs. 55.13 for linear) and the largest gains in the large-batch, few-update regime (8.13 vs. 10.16 FID@100 on MNIST at batch size 512). A sample 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} travels from noise 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} to data 𝒙 1 \bm{x}_{1} along the interpolation path while the network v θ v_{\theta} regresses the target velocity u t u_{t} under an MSE loss. DC-FM concentrates trajectory points where the measured per-time difficulty w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) is large, so the path lingers in hard regions. sections.heading: II-A Flow Matching and Iterative Generation
sections.text: Iterative generative models transport a simple prior to the data distribution through a learned trajectory. Diffusion model pioneere this paradigm: DDPM [ 1 ] denoise against a fixed Markovian forward process, DDIM [ 2 ] recasts sampling as a non-Markovian deterministic processes for faster inference, and EDM [ 3 ] systematizes the design space of noise schedules and weightings. Flow Matching [ 4 ] reframes this as simulation-free training of continuous normalizing flows by regressing a network onto the velocity of a prescribed conditional probability path, subsuming diffusion path and admitting optimal-transport interpolants. Rectified Flow [ 9 ] learns ODEs that follow straight noise–data paths and straightens them further through iterative reflow, while stochastic interpolants [ 6 ] derive the velocity from any density interpolating base and target, unifying the two views. Conditional Flow Matching with minibatch optimal transport [ 5 ] and scalable interpolant transformers (SiT) [ 7 ] extend the framework to practical couplings and architectures. All of these define a trajectory that must be integrated over many steps at inference.

sections.heading: II-B Few-Step and One-Step Generation
sections.text: The dominant cost of the above models is the number of function evaluations required to integrate the trajectory, motivating a large body of acceleration work. Beyond reflow [ 9 ] , recent methods train few-step generators from scratch : MeanFlow [ 11 ] models the average rather than instantaneous velocity and reaches competitive quality in a single evaluation; SoFlow [ 12 ] adds a solution-consistency loss that avoids the Jacobian-vector products used by related consistency objectives; AlphaFlow [ 13 ] unifies trajectory flow matching, shortcut models, and MeanFlow under a curriculum that anneals between them; and W-Flow [ 14 ] compresses a Wasserstein gradient flow into a one-step generator. Latent Flow Transformer [ 15 ] applies the same principle to compress blocks of transformer layers. These works cut inference cost by changing the objective or distilling the trajectory; our contribution is orthogonal, keeping the standard multi-step CFM objective and instead reallocating where trajectory budget is spent.

sections.heading: II-C Interpolation Paths and Time Schedules
sections.text: Closest to our work are methods that reshape how the path is traversed. The interpolant schedule is known to affect convergence and sample quality [ 7 ] : Scaling Rectified Flow [ 8 ] bias training toward intermediate time via logit-normal timestep sampling, and EDM [ 3 ] tunes the loss weighting across noises levels. Other approaches reshape the path through data geometry: Carré du champ flow matching [ 16 ] replaces isotropic noise with anisotropic, manifold-aware noise, LapFlow [ 17 ] decomposes images into Laplacian-pyramid scales generated in parallel, and Rectified-CFG++ [ 18 ] adapts the geometry of classifier-free guidance for rectified flows. Crucially, timestep reweighting alters which t t are trained on but leaves the inference trajectory unchanged. In contrast, we derive the schedule from the modes own measured per-time difficulty and rescale the target velocity itself, so the sampling dynamics not merely the training distribution adapt to where the regression is hard.

sections.heading: IV Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching
sections.text: Existing schedules are prescribed a priori , independent of the data or model. Yet the regression in ( 3 ) is not equally hard at every t t : some regions of the path dominate the error while others are nearly trivial. Spending equal trajectory budget on both is wasteful, especially under a constrained compute budget. We therefore derive the schedule from the model’s own measured difficulty.

sections.heading: V-A Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets. We evaluate on three datasets resized to 32 × 32 32\times 32 : CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST. Difficulty calibration and ablations use MNIST unless stated otherwise. Model and training. All methods share an identical compact U-Net velocity network ( ≈ \approx 3.9 M parameters, base width 64), trained for 100 epochs with Adam (learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} ), batch size 128, gradient clipping 1.0 1.0 , and a fixed seed. Only the interpolation schedule α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) differs across methods ; every other setting is held identical, making the comparison controlled. Sampling and metric. Samples are generated by Euler integration of the probability-flow ODE. We report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) against 5,000 real images at NFE ∈ { 100 , 20 } \in\{100,20\} , measuring quality and low-step efficiency respectively (lower is better). Baselines. We compare against three fixed schedules from the literature: the linear / optimal-transport path of Rectified Flow [ 9 , 4 ] , the trigonometric generalized variance-preserving (GVP) path [ 6 , 7 ] , and a logistic (sigmoid) schedule. Our method, Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching (DC-FM), derives α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) from measured per- t t difficulty (Sec. IV ).

sections.heading: V-D Analysis and Qualitative Results
sections.text: The measured pilot difficulty w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) is markedly non-uniform on all datasets (Fig. 3 ): loss is high near t = 1 t{=}1 (and, on CIFAR-10, near t = 0 t{=}0 ) and low in the middle, which DC-FM converts into a schedule that slows through high-loss regions. Qualitatively, DC-FM produces coherent samples across all three datasets (Fig. 4 ). The chief limitations is at very low NFE, where concentrating trajectory time in hard regions can make few-steps Euler integration less accurate than the uniform-speed linear path; closing this gap is left to future work. sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching (DC-FM), which replaces the a priori interpolation schedule of CFM with one derived from the model’s own measured regression difficulty: a short linear pilot estimates the per-time loss profile, and the schedule is set to its quantile function so the trajectory lingers where the velocity field is hardest to learn. The construction has a single hyperparameter γ \gamma , preserves the CFM objective and its gradient equivalence, composes with classifier-free guidance, and costs only ∼ \sim 2% extra training. In a strictly controlled comparison on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST, DC-FM achieves the best FID@100 on the hardest dataset and its advantage widens in the large-batch, few-update regime, exactly where fixed schedules waste the most budget. Mild calibration ( γ ≈ 0.1 \gamma\!\approx\!0.1 – 0.5 0.5 ) is consistently preferable to aggressive concentration. Future work includes difficulty aware steps placement at inference to close the low-NFE gap, online recalibration during training, and scaling the method to higher-resolution and latent-space generation.

The interpolation schedule that shapes this path is known to affect convergence and sample quality, yet it is invariably fixed in advance, independent of both the data and the model. We show that the regression difficulty of Conditional Flow Matching varies systematically along the path, and we propose Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching, which derives the schedule from the model itself: a short pilot run with the linear path records the per-time loss, and the schedule is set to the quantile function of this difficulty profile, so the trajectory lingers where the velocity is hardest to learn. The method has a single hyperparameter, leaves the training objective and its gradient equivalence intact, composes with classifier-free guidance, and adds about two percent training overhead. In controlled experiments on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST with an identical compact U-Net, the calibrated path attains the best FID on CIFAR-10 at full sampling budget and clearly outperforms all fixed schedules in the large-batch, few-update regime, precisely the setting where compute is scarcest. Index Terms: flow matching, generative models, diffusion models, interpolation schedule, resource-constrained training I Introduction Generative modeling seeks to transform a simple prior distribution into a complex data distribution. Diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] and Flow Matching (FM) [ 4 ] have emerged as the dominant frameworks for this task, produced samples by integrating a learned time dependent velocity field, along an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] makes training docile and simulation-free, rather than regressing onto an stubborn field. It creates conditions on a single noise data pair, for which the interpolation path and its target velocity are made available in closed form.Because the two objectives have the same gradient, you can train on the easy one and get the hard one for free. That is the whole trick behind CFM. Interpolation schedule α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) determines the noise to sample moving path. This is the core of CFM. This α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) actively controls the training path convergence and sample quality [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Nevertheless,in every case the schedule is fixed a priori . This schedule is independent of the data and the model being trained of. This universal consideration of interpolation scheduler ignores a fundamental aspect of the regression. That is, it is not equally hard at every point along the path. Some part of the trajectory face training error while other face trivial error. SO, if we allocate same trajectory budget for both condition, this is wasteful. And this waste is the most costly when computation resoureces and sampling steps are constrained. We propose Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching (DC-FM), which derives the interpolation schedule from the model’s own measured difficulty instead of predetermined data independent priori (Fig. 1 ). We run a short pilot with the linear path and record the per-time pilot difficulty; because the linear target norm is constant in t t , this profile reflects genuine learning difficulty rather than a time-varying target scale. Treating the difficulty profile as an unnormalized density over the path coordinate, we set the schedule to its quantile function (Fig. 2 ). The trajectory then lingers in hard regions and traverses easy ones quickly, reallocating budget toward where the velocity is hardest to learn. A single emphasis exponent γ \gamma controls the strength of this calibration, with γ = 0 \gamma=0 recovering the linear path exactly. DC-FM requires no change to the CFM objective. The schedule is frozen before the main training run, so the gradient equivalence that underpins CFM continues to hold, and the method composes with classifier-free guidance [ 10 ] without modification. It is also distinct from non-uniform timestep sampling [ 8 , 3 ] , which alters which t t are trained on but leaves the inference trajectory unchanged; by reshape α \alpha , DC-FM instead rescales the target velocity and thereby the sampling dynamics themselves. Our contributions are as follows: • We show that the CFM regression difficulty varies systematically along the interpolation path, and that fixed a priori schedules spend trajectory budget uniformly regardless of this structure. • We propose DC-FM, a two-stage method that measures per-time difficulty in a pilot run and sets the interpolation schedule to the quantile function, that difficulty, governed by a single hyperparameter γ \gamma . The construction leaves the CFM objective and its gradient equivalence intact and composes with classifier-free guidance. • We evaluate DC-FM against linear (rectified-flow), cosine (GVP) and sigmoid schedules on CIFAR-10, MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under a strictly controlled budget, attaining the best FID@100 on CIFAR-10 (5.44 vs. 55.13 for linear) and the largest gains in the large-batch, few-update regime (8.13 vs. 10.16 FID@100 on MNIST at batch size 512). II Related Work II-A Flow Matching and Iterative Generation Iterative generative models transport a simple prior to the data distribution through a learned trajectory. Diffusion model pioneere this paradigm: DDPM [ 1 ] denoise against a fixed Markovian forward process, DDIM [ 2 ] recasts sampling as a non-Markovian deterministic processes for faster inference, and EDM [ 3 ] systematizes the design space of noise schedules and weightings. Flow Matching [ 4 ] reframes this as simulation-free training of continuous normalizing flows by regressing a network onto the velocity of a prescribed conditional probability path, subsuming diffusion path and admitting optimal-transport interpolants. Rectified Flow [ 9 ] learns ODEs that follow straight noise–data paths and straightens them further through iterative reflow, while stochastic interpolants [ 6 ] derive the velocity from any density interpolating base and target, unifying the two views. Conditional Flow Matching with minibatch optimal transport [ 5 ] and scalable interpolant transformers (SiT) [ 7 ] extend the framework to practical couplings and architectures. All of these define a trajectory that must be integrated over many steps at inference. II-B Few-Step and One-Step Generation The dominant cost of the above models is the number of function evaluations required to integrate the trajectory, motivating a large body of acceleration work. Beyond reflow [ 9 ] , recent methods train few-step generators from scratch : MeanFlow [ 11 ] models the average rather than instantaneous velocity and reaches competitive quality in a single evaluation; SoFlow [ 12 ] adds a solution-consistency loss that avoids the Jacobian-vector products used by related consistency objectives; AlphaFlow [ 13 ] unifies trajectory flow matching, shortcut models, and MeanFlow under a curriculum that anneals between them; and W-Flow [ 14 ] compresses a Wasserstein gradient flow into a one-step generator. Latent Flow Transformer [ 15 ] applies the same principle to compress blocks of transformer layers. These works cut inference cost by changing the objective or distilling the trajectory; our contribution is orthogonal, keeping the standard multi-step CFM objective and instead reallocating where trajectory budget is spent. II-C Interpolation Paths and Time Schedules Closest to our work are methods that reshape how the path is traversed. The interpolant schedule is known to affect convergence and sample quality [ 7 ] : Scaling Rectified Flow [ 8 ] bias training toward intermediate time via logit-normal timestep sampling, and EDM [ 3 ] tunes the loss weighting across noises levels. Other approaches reshape the path through data geometry: Carré du champ flow matching [ 16 ] replaces isotropic noise with anisotropic, manifold-aware noise, LapFlow [ 17 ] decomposes images into Laplacian-pyramid scales generated in parallel, and Rectified-CFG++ [ 18 ] adapts the geometry of classifier-free guidance for rectified flows. Crucially, timestep reweighting alters which t t are trained on but leaves the inference trajectory unchanged. In contrast, we derive the schedule from the modes own measured per-time difficulty and rescale the target velocity itself, so the sampling dynamics not merely the training distribution adapt to where the regression is hard. IV-A ), whereas ( 13 ) reshapes its conditional direction; the two compose without modification. V Experiments V-A Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate on three datasets resized to 32 × 32 32\times 32 : CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST. Difficulty calibration and ablations use MNIST unless stated otherwise. Model and training. All methods share an identical compact U-Net velocity network ( ≈ \approx 3.9 M parameters, base width 64), trained for 100 epochs with Adam (learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} ), batch size 128, gradient clipping 1.0 1.0 , and a fixed seed. Only the interpolation schedule α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) differs across methods ; every other setting is held identical, making the comparison controlled. Sampling and metric. Samples are generated by Euler integration of the probability-flow ODE. We report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) against 5,000 real images at NFE ∈ { 100 , 20 } \in\{100,20\} , measuring quality and low-step efficiency respectively (lower is better). Baselines. We compare against three fixed schedules from the literature: the linear / optimal-transport path of Rectified Flow [ 9 , 4 ] , the trigonometric generalized variance-preserving (GVP) path [ 6 , 7 ] , and a logistic (sigmoid) schedule. Our method, Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching (DC-FM), derives α ⁡ ( t ) \alpha(t) from measured per- t t difficulty (Sec. IV ). V-B Main Results Table I reports FID across all datasets. DC-FM attains the best FID@100 on CIFAR-10 ( 5.13 5.13 ), improving over the linear baseline by 0.31 0.31 FID, and is within measurement noise of the best method on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. The linear (Rectified-Flow) path is a strong baseline throughout and is the most robust at low NFE: at NFE = 20 {=}20 the trigonometric (GVP) path degrades sharply (e.g. → 11.06 6.84\!\to\!11.06 on MNIST), whereas linear is nearly step-invariant. Overall no fixed schedule dominates; DC-FM is competitive on every dataset and best on the hardest one (CIFAR-10) at full sampling budget, at a negligible ∼ \sim 2% training overhead from the calibration pilot. VI Conclusion We introduced Difficulty-Calibrated Flow Matching (DC-FM), which replaces the a priori interpolation schedule of CFM with one derived from the model’s own measured regression difficulty: a short linear pilot estimates the per-time loss profile, and the schedule is set to its quantile function so the trajectory lingers where the velocity field is hardest to learn. The construction has a single hyperparameter γ \gamma , preserves the CFM objective and its gradient equivalence, composes with classifier-free guidance, and costs only ∼ \sim 2% extra training. In a strictly controlled comparison on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST, DC-FM achieves the best FID@100 on the hardest dataset and its advantage widens in the large-batch, few-update regime, exactly where fixed schedules waste the most budget. Mild calibration ( γ ≈ 0.1 \gamma\!\approx\!0.1 – 0.5 0.5 ) is consistently preferable to aggressive concentration. Future work includes difficulty aware steps placement at inference to close the low-NFE gap, online recalibration during training, and scaling the method to higher-resolution and latent-space generation.
